opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. With traditional machine learning, evaluation was relatively well defined. You had a specific task, say classifying images or predicting loan defaults, and a dataset drawn from roughly the same distribution you'd see in deployment. You held out a test set, measured accuracy or some other metric, and that number told you a fair amount about how the model would behave in the real world. It wasn't perfect, since distribution shift was always a concern, but the gap between the benchmark and the use case was manageable.

Foundation models break that in several ways. First, they're general purpose. The same model might be used for writing code, summarizing legal documents, tutoring a student, or giving medical information. There isn't one task to evaluate, so you're sampling a tiny slice of a huge space of possible uses and hoping it generalizes. Usually it doesn't map cleanly.

Second, there's contamination. These models are trained on huge swaths of the internet, so there's a real chance benchmark questions, or things very close to them, were in the training data. When a model does well on a test, it's hard to know whether it's reasoning or recognizing. We've seen cases where performance drops sharply when you perturb questions slightly or use problems published after the training cutoff.

Third, the outputs are open ended. Grading a classification is easy. Grading an essay, a piece of advice, or a multistep agentic workflow is much harder. People increasingly use other models as judges, which brings its own biases.

Fourth, and this is the one I emphasize most, benchmarks measure capability, but what we care about is usefulness and impact in real settings. A model can ace a bar exam style test, yet that tells you little about whether it can do a lawyer's job, because most of that job isn't answering exam questions. Real work involves context, judgment, interacting with people, and knowing what you don't know. The leap from "scores well on a benchmark" to "will transform this profession" is where a lot of the hype comes from, and it's often unjustified.

Finally, there's a sociotechnical piece. How a model performs depends heavily on how people use it: how they prompt it, whether they check its outputs, what workflow it's embedded in. So evaluating the model in isolation is often the wrong unit of analysis. We need more evaluations that look at the whole system, including the humans, and more evidence from actual deployments rather than leaderboards.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts traditional models’ specific tasks with foundation models’ general-purpose use across many tasks, describing their possible uses as a huge space that benchmarks sample only slightly.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. I think the core of it comes down to one word: generality. With a traditional machine learning model, you built it to do one thing. You have a training distribution, you hold out a test set from that same distribution, you measure accuracy, and that number tells you something meaningful about how the model will perform in the setting you actually care about. The whole evaluation paradigm was designed around that narrow task framing, and it works reasonably well there.

Foundation models break that in a few ways. First, they're meant to be used for an open-ended, essentially unbounded set of tasks, most of which the developer never anticipated. So the question "how good is this model?" doesn't really have a single answer. Good at what? For whom? In what context? A benchmark score on, say, a question-answering dataset tells you very little about whether the model will be useful to a lawyer drafting a contract or a kid doing their homework.

Second, there's the contamination problem. These models are trained on enormous swaths of the internet, and benchmarks are published on the internet. So you very often can't tell whether the model actually has some capability or whether it has memorized the test set. The train-test split, which was the bedrock of ML evaluation, is just much harder to guarantee. And the labs usually don't disclose training data, so outsiders can't check.

Third, the thing we actually want to know is about real-world performance, and benchmarks are at best a proxy for that. Sayash Kapoor and I have been looking at this a lot in the context of AI agents. A model might score beautifully on a static benchmark but fall over when it has to act in an environment, deal with ambiguity, recover from errors, or interact with a person over many turns. The gap between benchmark performance and deployment performance is much wider than it was for narrow models, and we don't have good tools for measuring that gap.

And then there's the fact that evaluation itself is now partly a prompting and scaffolding problem. Change the prompt, change the number of samples, change the tools the model has access to, and you get a different number. So comparisons between models often aren't apples to apples, and leaderboards end up measuring the evaluation setup as much as the model.

So I'd say traditional ML evaluation was a solved-ish problem for a narrow question, and foundation models have turned it into a largely unsolved problem for a much broader one. That's not a reason for despair, but it does mean we should be a lot more humble about what a benchmark number actually means.

r001.rationale: It contrasts traditional models built for one task with foundation models intended for an open-ended, essentially unbounded set of tasks.

astra-6.text:
The biggest difference is that with a traditional machine learning model, you usually have a fairly well-defined task. You’re predicting whether an email is spam, for example. You can collect a test set, decide what counts as a correct answer, and measure how well the model performs.

With a foundation model, the range of possible uses is open-ended. The same model might be used to write code, summarize a document, or help someone think through a medical question. There isn’t one test set—or even one definition of success—that captures all of that.

And performance depends on how you interact with the model. The prompt, the context you provide, and whether the model is connected to tools can all change the result. So we have to distinguish between evaluating a model in the abstract and evaluating a particular application built around it.

Benchmarks can tell us something useful, but the difficult step is connecting a benchmark score to what we actually care about: Will this system work reliably for these users, on these tasks, under these conditions? That gap is much larger with foundation models.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts traditional models’ well-defined task with foundation models’ open-ended range of uses, giving examples of varied tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
The big difference is that with a traditional machine learning model, you usually have a fairly well-defined task. You’re predicting whether an email is spam, for example. You can put together a test set, specify a metric, and get a reasonably useful picture of how well the model works.

With foundation models, the whole promise is that one model can be used for an enormous range of tasks, including tasks its developers didn’t anticipate. So what would it mean to evaluate that model? You can’t boil all of those uses down to a single accuracy number.

And even within a particular task, performance depends on how you prompt the model, what tools you give it, and how people interact with it. A benchmark measures one particular setup. Moving from that result to a claim about how useful or reliable the model will be in practice is a much bigger leap. We have to evaluate the system in the context of its intended use, rather than treating a benchmark score as a general measure of capability.

r001.rationale: It contrasts traditional models’ well-defined task with foundation models’ use across an enormous, open-ended range of tasks.
